content:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture confirmed on Wednesday the first known detection of the flesh-eating parasite known as the New World screwworm in U.S. wildlife — an elk in Pecos County, Texas. The animal was on a game ranch and was reported after being harvested by a hunter, the USDA said in a statement.

New Mexico authorities separately confirmed a case of New World screwworm in a beef cow in Otero County, New Mexico, the same day.

The Texas Animal Health Commission will modify a previously established infested zone around the finding, and the USDA and the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department are conducting additional wildlife surveillance in the area, the USDA said. In New Mexico, officials established a minimum 12.4-mile (20 km) radius infested zone around the affected animal’s location; within that zone, animals must be inspected and, if necessary, treated before being moved within or out of the area. State and federal officials are expanding surveillance and fly-trapping around both locations to determine whether the pest has spread beyond the affected animals.

A pest the U.S. eradicated decades ago

The New World screwworm was eradicated from the United States decades ago, but the pest has surged north from Central America through Mexico. Its northward march prompted Washington to impose a more than year-long ban on Mexican cattle imports. The U.S. halted livestock imports from Mexico last year to keep the screwworm out, but resumed trade in August at an Arizona port as part of a phased reopening plan.

The import halt tightened U.S. cattle supplies and contributed to a rise in beef prices to record highs for American consumers — a pressure Texas ranchers and South Texas families feel at the grocery checkout every week.

What it means for Texas ranch country

The wildlife detection changes the picture. Until now, the outbreak conversation centered on livestock and imports; a screwworm case in wild game suggests the parasite may be moving through the landscape on its own, not just arriving in imported herds. That is why the surveillance radius and fly-trapping matter: screwworms infest the wounds of warm-blooded animals, and the larval feeding can be fatal if untreated. Ranchers in West Texas — and across the state, including Webb County’s ranching community — are being told to watch animals closely for signs of infestation and report suspicious cases to animal health authorities.

title: Flesh-Eating Screwworm Found in U.S. Wildlife for First Time: Elk in Pecos County, Texas
